pool.prompt: Under 29 CFR 1910.268(g)(1), fall protection is required when working on a pole at what height above ground?
choices: 6 feet (same as construction industry)
10 feet
4 feet
Fall protection is required only when using a bucket truck
pool.explanation: 29 CFR 1910.268(g)(1) — the telecommunications standard — triggers the fall protection requirement at more than 4 feet above ground on poles. This differs from 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M (construction), which triggers at 6 feet. Telecom OSP work falls under 1910 (general industry), not 1926 (construction).

pool.prompt: A worker's body belt and pole strap are the ONLY fall protection they use at their work position on a 40-foot pole. Their gaff pulls out of rotten wood. What happens?
choices: The pole strap (positioning system) automatically arrests the fall by holding the worker against the pole
The body belt automatically deploys an energy-absorbing lanyard to arrest the fall
The positioning system may not catch the fall — only a PFAS (full-body harness + arrest lanyard) provides fall arrest protection
The 4-foot rule means fall protection isn't required at 40 feet
pool.explanation: A positioning system (body belt + pole strap) is designed to hold the worker at the work position — not to arrest a fall. If the gaff pulls out and the body shifts suddenly, the positioning strap may slip rather than catch the fall. Only a PFAS is designed to arrest a fall and limit the arrest force to 1,800 lbf or less.
pool.citation: 29 CFR 1910.268(g)(1); ANSI Z359.1/Z359.11 (body belt restrictions within the Z359 series).

pool.prompt: When working in a bucket truck aerial lift, where must a worker's fall protection lanyard be attached?
choices: To a fixed anchor point outside the basket, such as the pole being worked on
To the boom or basket of the aerial lift itself
To the truck's frame at ground level
Fall protection is not required in a bucket truck
pool.explanation: Attaching to the boom or basket ensures the fall protection travels with the worker if the truck moves. Attaching to a fixed structure outside the basket (pole, crossarm) can pull the worker out of the basket if the truck repositions — a common and fatal error.

pool.prompt: An OSHA interpretation letter on 29 CFR 1910.268 addresses telecom workers reaching their work position on a pole. What does it establish?
choices: No fall protection is required at any point on a utility pole
Fall protection is required at all times during both climbing and at the work position
Fall protection is required at the work position (if more than 4 ft up); climbing to reach that position may be done without fall protection ('free-climbing')
Free-climbing is permitted only for poles shorter than 30 feet
pool.explanation: The letter addresses a telecom pole-climbing scenario and confirms the distinction: 1910.268 permits employees to free-climb (move) to their work position on poles without fall protection during the climb itself, but requires fall protection at the work position — where the worker stops to perform a task — if it is more than 4 feet above ground.

pool.prompt: What is the maximum arresting force (MAF) a full-body harness/PFAS system is permitted to expose a falling worker to, per OSHA/ANSI Z359 requirements?
choices: 800 lbf
There is no maximum — any force that stops the fall is acceptable
pool.explanation: OSHA and ANSI Z359 both limit maximum arresting force to 1,800 lbf (8 kN) for a full-body harness system. Energy-absorbing lanyards and self-retracting lifelines are engineered and tested to stay within this limit.
pool.citation: OSHA/ANSI Z359 maximum arresting force standard.

pool.prompt: 29 CFR 1926.500/1926.502 (the CONSTRUCTION fall-protection standard) has prohibited body belts for fall ARREST use since January 1, 1998. Telecom OSP work falls under 1910.268 (general industry), not 1926 — so what governs the body-belt-vs-harness question for a telecom pole crew?
choices: Nothing — 1910.268 has no equivalent requirement, so body belts remain acceptable for fall arrest in telecom work
The 1926.502 date and rule apply directly to telecom work too, since OSHA construction rules always override 1910 general industry rules

1910.268 doesn't import the 1926.502 date, but a full-body harness meeting ANSI Z359.11 is still the applicable requirement for any PFAS (fall arrest) used in telecom pole work — a body belt/pole strap remains acceptable ONLY as a positioning system, never for fall arrest
Fall arrest equipment requirements are entirely voluntary for telecom crews
pool.explanation: The January 1, 1998 body-belt prohibition is specifically a 29 CFR 1926.500/1926.502 CONSTRUCTION provision and does not directly bind 1910.268 (general industry) telecom work — this is a real cross-standard distinction, not an assumption. However, the practical outcome for telecom crews is the same: a body belt/pole strap positioning system is not tested or designed for fall arrest, and ANSI Z359.11 (full-body harness standard, referenced across the fall-protection industry regardless of which CFR part applies) is the applicable requirement whenever a PFAS is used. Do not cite the 1926.502 date as if it were a 1910.268 rule.
pool.citation: 29 CFR 1926.500/1926.502 (body belt fall-arrest prohibition, effective January 1, 1998 — a CONSTRUCTION-specific rule, not directly applicable to 1910.268 telecom work); ANSI Z359.11 (full-body harness standard, cross-industry).

pool.prompt: Why is the fall protection height trigger different for telecom pole work (1910.268, >4 ft) versus general construction (1926 Subpart M, 6 ft)?
choices: It's an inconsistency with no regulatory basis and either number may be used
Telecom OSP field work falls under 1910 (general industry standards), not 1926 (construction standards) — different regulatory subparts set different trigger heights for their respective industries
The 4-foot trigger only applies to underground work, not aerial
1910.268 was written before 1926 Subpart M and is now obsolete
pool.explanation: Telecom OSP work is classified under 29 CFR 1910 (general industry) rather than 1926 (construction), and 1910.268(g)(1) sets its own trigger height (>4 ft) specific to pole work — distinct from the 6-ft trigger in the construction fall-protection subpart. Crews must know which regulatory framework applies to their specific work.

pool.prompt: What is the functional difference between a POSITIONING system (body belt + pole strap) and a PFAS (Personal Fall Arrest System)?
choices: They are the same thing with different names

A positioning system holds the worker at a fixed work position (not designed to catch a fall); a PFAS (full-body harness + energy-absorbing lanyard/SRL) is engineered specifically to arrest a fall and limit arrest force
A PFAS is only used for aerial lifts; positioning systems are only used on poles
A positioning system is stronger and provides more fall protection than a PFAS
pool.explanation: A positioning system lets a worker lean back and work hands-free at a fixed point — it is not tested or designed to arrest a fall from height. A PFAS (full-body harness anchored via an energy-absorbing lanyard or SRL) is specifically engineered and tested to stop a fall while limiting the arrest force to 1,800 lbf or less. Using a positioning system as the sole protection against an actual fall is a critical safety gap.
